<!-- Generated by scripts/build-site-pages.py from docs/vcon.md — do not edit. Edit the source page and re-run the script; site_pages_mirror_is_current fails if this file is stale. -->

Something downstream wants the call rather than the packets.

- Examples are a conversation archive, a compliance store, or an agent that reasons over calls.
- Hand any of them a pcap, and you have made the decoding their problem.
- vCon is the interchange container those systems already read.
- sipnab writes one per observed dialog.

**The short version.** A vCon is a JSON object about one conversation. It holds:

- the parties,
- what passed between them,
- what some tool concluded about it.

sipnab fills that shape from signaling it watched go past a tap. Each container carries:

- the SIP ladder,
- the parties the `From` and `To` headers named,
- a diagnosis of the call,
- a statement of what the capture missed. This is in two places, deliberately.

When the run retained the RTP payload, the container also carries the audio, inline.

- It is the whole call, from its first frame, unless a retention limit cut it.
- If a limit cut it, the container says so (see [Audio retention budget](@/docs/config.md#audio-retention-budget)).
- None of them carries any claim that somebody consented to anything.
- None carries a signature unless you configure a rule to encrypt its containers (see [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes)).

**A sipnab vCon records what an instrument
saw, not what the parties said.** Read [What may you conclude](#someone-handed-you-a-sipnab-vcon-what-may-you-conclude),
below, before you trust a container. It is the one part of this page to read first.

## What a vCon is, and what sipnab is to it

vCon means "Conversation Data Container". It travels between systems as four arrays:

- `parties`: who took part.
- `dialog`: what passed between them, and when.
- `analysis`: what a machine concluded about that.
- `attachments`: documents riding alongside.

The ecosystem around the format assumes a **recorder**.

- A recorder is something inside the conversation.
- It took the media from a party, and it can say what that party agreed to.
- A recorder can write *"I received this audio from the caller."*

sipnab was never inside the conversation. It reads a mirror port.

- So the strongest sentence it can honestly write is *"I saw packets claiming to be this
  call go past this tap."*
- Those two sentences look alike in JSON. They mean entirely different things.

So sipnab emits **observer** vCons.

- The container names sipnab as a passive party.
- That party contributes to a record somebody else owns. The format itself defines this role.
- The container stops there. It never claims to **be** the conversation.
- [The Phase 0 decision](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/design/vcon.md) argues that position in full. That includes
  every refusal summarized further down this page.

## Produce one

The export sits behind the non-default `vcon` Cargo feature. So a stock build
does not carry it. The `full` feature includes it. On its own, it looks like
this:

```sh
cargo build --release --features vcon
```

The feature is non-default for the reason every capture-side feature is:

- A container that leaves the machine is a publication surface.
- A capture tool should not grow one unless an operator asks for it.

sipnab builds a container from one dialog. Every surface that offers the
export writes the same bytes. Pick the door that suits you:

| You are | Ask this way | Answers with |
|---|---|---|
| At a shell, reading a capture file | `sipnab -N -I call.pcap --export-vcon 'CALL-ID' --vcon-out out.json` | the container in `out.json` |
| At a shell, wanting it on stdout | `sipnab -N -I call.pcap --export-vcon 'CALL-ID'` | the container on stdout |
| An agent holding an MCP session, one call | the `export_vcon` tool, with `call_id` | one container, its SHA-256, and what the capture missed |
| An agent holding an MCP session, a set | the `export_vcon` tool, with `filter` | one entry per matching dialog, bounded by `--mcp-max-rows` |
| An agent checking a container before sending it | the `validate_vcon` tool | a verdict against the working group's draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema, with every finding named |
| A program over HTTP | `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` | `200` and the container, or `404` |
| Rust, in-process | `sipnab::output::vcon::export_dialog` | a `Vcon` value |

Two notes on the CLI pair:

- `--vcon-out` requires `--export-vcon`. A path with nothing to write to it is a mistake. sipnab would rather name it than
  ignore it.
- sipnab refuses a `--vcon-out` that names the capture it is reading. An export that overwrites its own evidence is not an export.

On a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`), `--export-vcon` writes the call's
container when that call ends.

- It uses the same timing the spool below follows:
  - the call has ended,
  - it has been quiet for five seconds,
  - sipnab keeps capturing meanwhile.
- sipnab writes a call that has not ended once it has carried no SIP
  and no RTP for 120 seconds.
  - It writes it again if it changes later (see
    [When the call had not ended](#when-the-call-had-not-ended)).
- A live capture that you stop writes nothing.
  - So a call that had not ended and settled leaves no
    `--vcon-out` file behind.
- A live run can end on its own (`--duration`, `--autostop`).
  - It then writes the call, if it was not already written.
  - It still fails if that Call-ID never appeared.
- With `-I`, sipnab writes the container at the end of the run, as before.

The TUI does not offer the export.

- It is a live view of a running capture.
- It points at the doors above. Its help screen names the REST route and the
  feature flag.
- It does not grow a key binding. That binding would do nothing in a build
  without the feature.

Read on for what the container means once you hold one.

## Write calls by rule

A `[[vcon.rule]]` in the config file pairs a filter with two things:

- the directory its containers go to,
- what they carry.

A run can hold several rules. sipnab writes a call that matches several rules once per rule, into each rule's directory.

```toml
[filters]
support = "to.user == '7000' OR header.X-Queue == 'support'"

[[vcon.rule]]
name  = "support-with-audio"
when  = "@support"
dir   = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio = "inline"

[[vcon.rule]]
name  = "all-calls"
when  = "method == 'INVITE'"
dir   = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/all"
```

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `name` | The rule's name, used in the run's report and to pick its spool over REST and MCP. 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, `-` or `_` |
| `when` | The filter a call must match. [Named filters](@/docs/filter-dsl.md#named-filters) work here as `@name` |
| `dir` | The directory the rule writes to. sipnab creates it if it is missing |
| `audio` | `inline`: the audio the run retained travels inside the container, within `--vcon-max-inline-media`. `omit` (the default): no audio, and the container records `media: "not-considered"`. A rule with `inline` turns audio retention on for the run, as `--retain-audio` does |
| `audio` = `url` | sipnab writes the audio to a WAV file beside the container, `<container name>.wav`, and the container's recording names `audio_url_base` followed by that file name, with the `content_hash` of the WAV file and no body; the completeness block records `media: "referenced"`. sipnab writes the file and serves nothing: the operator's storage serves the URL. Turns audio retention on, as `inline` does |
| `audio_url_base` | For `audio = "url"`: the HTTPS base URL that serves the WAV files. Required with `url`; core-04 section 2.4.1 requires HTTPS for a reference |
| `max_inline_media_mib` | The largest audio this rule's containers inline, in MiB. sipnab writes a call above it without its audio and the container records `media: "refused-over-budget"`. Unset: `--vcon-max-inline-media` |
| `live_audio` | `true`: serve each matching call's audio while it is in progress, over the REST API. See [Hear a call while it is in progress](#hear-a-call-while-it-is-in-progress) |
| `live` | `true`: on a live capture, write each matching call's container as the call starts and rewrite it in place each time the call changes. See [Follow a call while it is in progress](#follow-a-call-while-it-is-in-progress) |
| `encrypt_to` | A PEM certificate. Set, the rule writes only the encrypted form, to that certificate's key. Needs `sign_key` and `sign_cert`. See [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes) |
| `sign_key`, `sign_cert` | The PEM RSA private key an encrypting rule signs with, and its certificate chain, leaf first |
| `compress` | For an encrypting rule: `none` (the default) or `gzip`, which signs the gzip of the vCon instead of the vCon. See [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes) |
| `sealed_updates` | What an encrypting rule writes when a call it already wrote changes: `new-uuid` (the default), `same-uuid` or `final-only`. No effect without `encrypt_to`. See [When an encrypted call changes](#when-an-encrypted-call-changes) |
| `grouping` | `leg` (the default): one container per dialog. `call`: one container per call, holding every leg the rule selects. See [Calls through a PBX or a B2BUA](#calls-through-a-pbx-or-a-b2bua) |

Other options work with rules:

- `--export-vcon-when` with `--export-vcon-dir` still works. It is one more
  rule beside the configured ones.
- `--since` and `--until` narrow every rule.
- `--content-deny-header` applies before every rule.
- Each rule's directory is a spool the forwarder can deliver. Run one `--vcon-forward` per directory.

A rule runs the same way as `--export-vcon-when`.

- With `-I`, sipnab writes every matching call at the end of the run.
- On a live capture, sipnab writes each call on the timing described under
  [When a container appears](#the-spool-contract-for-a-bridge-that-consumes-it).
  - It uses each rule's own record of what it has written.
- On a live capture, sipnab gives back a call's retained audio only once every `inline` rule that matches
  the call has written it.

sipnab checks every rule when it starts. It refuses to start, with exit code 1, and names the rule, when:

- a name is unusable or used twice,
- a rule has no `dir`,
- `audio` is not `inline`, `url` or `omit`,
- `grouping` is not `leg` or `call`,
- `when` does not resolve.

sipnab also refuses a rule with any other key. So a misspelled key cannot leave a rule that
writes nowhere.

A live capture with a rule refuses `--redact`, `--redact-map`
and `--content-deny-tombstone`. It does the same with `--export-vcon-when`.

The end of a run reports each rule on its own line, for example
`[[vcon.rule]] 'all-calls': Wrote 2 vCon container(s) to '/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/all'.`

### Calls through a PBX or a B2BUA

A call through a PBX or a B2BUA is two dialogs or more. There is one per leg, and each has
its own Call-ID.

sipnab ties the legs with the same correlation strategies that
`get_call_tree` and `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree` report:

- an identifier both legs carry. This is one of:
  - [RFC 7989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7989.html) `Session-ID`,
  - a header listed in [`[sip] xcid_headers`](@/docs/config.md#sip),
  - the SDP origin,
  - a charging vector,
  - a Via branch.
- when the legs share none, a timing guess from shared
  addresses and close start times.

With `grouping = "leg"`, the default, each leg is its own container.

- Every export adds a `sipnab-related-legs` attachment to a leg that has others. The exports are:
  - a rule,
  - `--export-vcon-when`,
  - `--export-vcon`,
  - REST `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon`,
  - MCP `export_vcon`.
- Its body lists each other leg, strongest tie first:

```json
{"legs": [{"uuid": "018bcfe5-6800-88c0-b9c0-24e4c93555ff",
           "strategy": "x_call_id", "identifier_match": true, "score": 100}]}
```

- `uuid` is the other leg's container uuid. It stays the same under
  `--redact`.
- `identifier_match` is `false` for a timing guess. A busy
  server can get a timing guess wrong.

With `grouping = "call"`, the rule writes one container per call. It holds
every leg the rule selects:

- the parties of each leg in leg order, then the sipnab observer, last;
- each leg's Dialog Objects in leg order;
- each leg's message trace, completeness attachment and analysis. These point at that leg's objects;
- with `audio = "inline"` or `"url"`, each leg's own two-channel recording.
  - Its `parties` maps each channel to a party of that leg. So every party of
    the call has a channel.
  - sipnab does not mix the legs into one file. They
    start at different times and can use different sample rates.
  - Each recording keeps the timing sipnab captured it with;
- a `sipnab-call-legs` attachment. It names:
  - each leg's signaling object,
  - every tie, with its strategy, `identifier_match` and score,
  - `truncated: true` when the call had more than 16 legs and the rest went into further
    containers.

More about the per-call container:

- The container has its own uuid, derived from every leg's Call-ID.
  - So it is the same each time sipnab exports the capture.
  - It differs from every leg container's uuid.
- sipnab names it after the earliest leg.
- A PBX can be the callee on one leg and the caller on the next.
  - It appears once in each leg's parties.
  - Nothing in the signaling proves the two are one party.
- Some legs are not in the container:
  - a leg the rule's `when` does not match,
  - a leg that a `--content-deny-header` withheld.
  - So write `when` to match every leg of the calls you want.
- On a live capture, sipnab writes a call once every leg the rule selects has ended or gone idle.
  - It writes it again when a leg changes.

`leg` is the default for this reason:

- A PBX that copies no identifier gives only one tie: the timing guess.
- Grouping on a wrong guess puts two unrelated calls in one container.
- A container written with `call` states every tie sipnab
  built it on. So a reader can see when that happened.

### Enrich a call before it is written

<!-- vale Google.Passive = YES -->

A `[[vcon.enrich]]` names a service of yours, such as a transcriber or a summarizer.

- sipnab sends that service each call of the rules it lists. It does this before it writes the
  call's container.
- sipnab appends the service's answer to the container's `analysis`. The answer is one or more Analysis
  Objects.
- sipnab chooses no model and runs none. The service is
  whatever you run at the URL or program you name.

```toml
[[vcon.rule]]
name  = "support"
when  = "@support"
dir   = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio = "inline"

[[vcon.enrich]]
name  = "transcribe"
rules = ["support"]
url   = "http://127.0.0.1:9000/transcribe"
timeout_secs = 120

[[vcon.enrich]]
name    = "summarize"
rules   = ["support"]
command = "/usr/local/bin/summarize-call"
send    = ["signaling"]
```

The services a rule names run in the order the config file lists them, one call
at a time.

- So sipnab sends a later service what an earlier one added.
- In the example, `summarize` reads the transcript `transcribe` returned.

**The request** is one JSON document, POSTed to `url` or written to the
`command`'s standard input:

```json
{"schema": "sipnab-enrichment-request/1", "service": "transcribe",
 "vcon": {"uuid": "...", "parties": [], "dialog": [], "analysis": []},
 "audio": [{"dialog": 0, "sip_call_id": "...", "mediatype": "audio/wav",
            "encoding": "base64url", "body": "UklGR..."}]}
```

- `vcon` is the container as sipnab writes it, with one exception. Its `analysis`
  holds only what earlier services added, not sipnab's own report.
  - It is present when `send` includes `signaling`.
- `audio` is present when `send` includes `audio` and the run retained the call's audio.
  - It holds one WAV per leg.
  - `dialog` names the leg's signaling Dialog Object.
  - Audio a key could not decrypt is never sent, because it is never decoded.

**The answer** is a JSON document with an `analysis` list. Each entry is a
core-04 Analysis Object:

```json
{"analysis": [{"type": "transcript", "vendor": "example-stt",
               "product": "stt-2", "encoding": "none",
               "mediatype": "text/plain", "body": "Hello, this is support..."}]}
```

Each Analysis Object must carry:

- `type`,
- `vendor`,
- `encoding` (`none`, `json` or `base64url`),
- `body`.

The shape of `body` follows its `encoding`.

- With `json` the body is any JSON value, as
  [section 2.3.2 of the core draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-2.3.2)
  defines it. sipnab keeps it as sent, a string included.
- With `none` or `base64url` the body must be a string.

`product`, `schema`, `mediatype` and `dialog` are optional. A missing `dialog` is the first leg's signaling object.

**A WTF transcription.** An Analysis Object of type `wtf_transcription` is a
transcription in the World Transcription Format of
[draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02).
sipnab checks it before it keeps it:

- `encoding` is `json` and the body is a JSON object, as
  [section 6.1 of the WTF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02#section-6.1)
  requires.
- The body has the three sections
  [section 4.2 of the WTF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02#section-4.2)
  requires, with the members
  [section 6.2.1 of the WTF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02#section-6.2.1)
  lists:
  - `transcript`: `text`, `language`, `duration` of 0 or more, and
    `confidence` from 0 to 1.
  - `segments`: each with a unique integer `id`, `start`, an `end` after
    `start`, `text`, and `confidence` from 0 to 1. A `speaker` is an integer
    or a string, and `words` is an array of integers.
  - `metadata`: `created_at`, `processed_at`, `provider` and `model`.
- The optional sections, `words`, `speakers`, `quality`, `extensions`,
  `alternatives`, `enrichments` and `streaming`, stay as the service sent them.

A container that holds a WTF transcription lists `wtf_transcription` in
`extensions`. It is not in `critical`:
[section 5.1 of the WTF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02#section-5.1)
classifies the extension as Compatible. An answer whose WTF transcription
fails the check is `malformed`, and its `detail` names what is wrong.

A transcriber can listen to a call on the
[live audio WebSocket](#hear-a-call-while-it-is-in-progress) while the call is
in progress:

- sipnab sends the service nothing during the call, and reads nothing from it.
- At the call's end, sipnab sends the service its `[[vcon.enrich]]` request.
- The service answers with its final transcription. A `streaming` section,
  [section 6.2.2.7 of the WTF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-howe-vcon-wtf-extension-02#section-6.2.2.7),
  can carry the session's `session_id` and `is_final: true`.
- Interim results stay with the service: sipnab has no route that receives
  them.

**What the container says.** Every enriched container carries a
`sipnab-enrichment` attachment. It lists each service sipnab sent it to, with:

- the service's name,
- its `target` (the URL or program),
- what was `sent`,
- the `outcome`,
- a `detail` in words, when it did not succeed,
- the indices in `analysis` of what it added.

So a reader of the container knows the call's audio left the host, and to which service.

| `outcome` | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `ok` | The service answered and sipnab appended its analysis |
| `failed` | sipnab could not reach the service, the service answered with an HTTP status other than 2xx, or the program exited non-zero |
| `timeout` | No answer within `timeout_secs` |
| `malformed` | The answer was not an `analysis` list of Analysis Objects; sipnab kept none of it |
| `queue-full` | On a live capture, 64 calls were already waiting for enrichment; sipnab sent nothing |

A service that does not succeed never loses the call:

- sipnab writes the container without that service's analysis.
- The attachment records why.
- The run says so on stderr. It names the service and the Call-ID. It also names the rule when it is a
  `[[vcon.rule]]`.

**When it runs.**

- With `-I`, sipnab enriches each matching call as it writes the
  call's container at the end of the run.
- On a live capture, a call that is due goes to a queue of at most 64 calls.
  - One worker enriches and writes them in turn.
  - So a slow service delays containers and never the capture.
  - sipnab writes a call that finds the queue full at once, unenriched, saying so.
- A live run that ends on its own (`--duration`) waits for the queue before it exits.
- A run that you stop does not wait. sipnab does not write the calls still waiting.

**What sipnab refuses at startup**, naming the enrichment:

- an unusable or repeated name
- no `rules`, or a rule name no `[[vcon.rule]]` defines
- both or neither of `url` and `command`
- an `http://` URL to anything but a loopback address (sipnab does not send
  call audio in the clear across a network)
- a `send` value other than `audio` and `signaling`
- a `timeout_secs` outside 1 to 3600
- an `auth_file` that does not load

sipnab also refuses a run with `--redact` and any `[[vcon.enrich]]`.

- sipnab sends a service the call as it captured it.
- It cannot replace anything the service answers with pseudonyms.

A dialog that `--content-deny-header` withheld is never sent to a service. It
is not exported at all.

### Hear a call while it is in progress

A rule with `live_audio = true` serves the audio of the calls it matches as
sipnab captures them.

- It serves them for a transcriber or any other program of yours.
- It serves them on the REST API (`--api`):

```toml
[[vcon.rule]]
name       = "support"
when       = "@support"
dir        = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio      = "inline"
live_audio = true
```

- `GET /v1/calls/live` lists the calls in progress the rule matches, and
  `GET /v1/calls/live/events` announces each one as a server-sent event.
- `GET /v1/calls/{call_id}/audio` is a WebSocket that sends the call's audio as
  16-bit PCM, one message per RTP packet, each direction a stream of its own,
  and closes when the call ends.

The `GET /v1/calls/:call_id/audio` section of the
[REST API reference](@/docs/api.md) gives every message.

- The audio is what sipnab retained, decoded. A `live_audio` rule turns
  retention on.
- Audio a key could not decrypt is never sent.
- A call that `--content-deny-header` withholds is neither listed nor served.

**Who may listen.**

- These routes need a token with the `audio` scope when the
  server authenticates (`sipnab --mint-token --token-scope audio`).
- No other scope reaches them. A `full` token and the static `--api-key` read dialogs
  and not call audio.
- On a loopback address, a server without keys serves them to
  any local process.
- Off loopback, sipnab refuses to start a `live_audio` rule unless the API has both:
  - TLS (`--api-tls-cert` and `--api-tls-key`),
  - a signing key (`--api-signing-key` or `--api-signing-key-file`).
- So the audio never crosses the network in the clear. It never goes to a client that has not proved it may
  hear it.

A [`[[vcon.enrich]]`](#enrich-a-call-before-it-is-written) service on the same
rule can return, at the call's end, what a transcriber produces during the call.
So the transcript is in the call's container.

### Follow a call while it is in progress

By default, a rule writes a call once, after it has ended (or gone quiet for
120 seconds).

A rule with `live = true` works differently:

- It writes the call's container as soon as sipnab sees the call start.
- It writes it again each time the call changes. It uses the same file name and
  the same `uuid`.
- So a program watching the spool sees the call as it goes:

```toml
[[vcon.rule]]
name = "follow"
when = "@support"
dir  = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/follow"
live = true
```

- Each write carries `updated_at`, the time of that write. `created_at` stays
  the time of the first write.
- Until the call ends, the completeness block records `call_ended: false`. The
  last write, after the call ends, records `true`.
- A container written while the call is in progress carries no audio, whatever
  `audio` says.
  - The write after the call ends carries it.
  - Enrichment (`[[vcon.enrich]]`) runs only on that last write.
- sipnab checks for changes every five seconds. So a write follows a change
  within about five seconds.
  - A sweep in which nothing changed writes nothing.
- `live` has an effect only on a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`).
  - With `-I`, the rule writes each call once, as any rule does, with no `updated_at`.

A forwarder delivers each rewrite as a new copy of the same container.

- A store that refuses a `uuid` it already holds needs the forwarder to replace it.
- See [What it does with each container](#what-it-does-with-each-container).
- A rule with `encrypt_to` does not rewrite in place by default. See
  [When an encrypted call changes](#when-an-encrypted-call-changes).

### Encrypt what a rule writes

A rule with `encrypt_to` writes each container in the encrypted form of
[draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 section 5.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-5.3).
So the spool, the forwarder's directories and the store hold nothing a reader
without the key can open:

```toml
[[vcon.rule]]
name       = "support"
when       = "@support"
dir        = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio      = "inline"
encrypt_to = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-recipient.crt"
sign_key   = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-signing.key"
sign_cert  = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-signing.crt"
```

The draft requires the producer to sign a container before it encrypts it. So the
rule does both, in this order:

- sipnab signs the container with `sign_key` (JWS, `RS256`).
  - The signature carries the `sign_cert` chain in `x5c`, in the signature's unprotected `header`.
    - [core-04 section 5.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-5.2) requires it there.
  - The protected header holds `alg`.
- sipnab encrypts that signed container to the RSA key in the `encrypt_to`
  certificate.
  - It uses JWE: `RSA-OAEP` for the content key, `A256CBC-HS512` for the
    content.
  - It uses a fresh content key for every write.

**Compress before encrypting.**

- `compress = "gzip"` compresses the vCon with gzip ([RFC 1952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952.html)) before sipnab signs it.
  - The JWS payload is then the gzip of the vCon, and the signature covers those bytes.
  - [core-04 section 5.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-5.2) allows this.
  - The encrypted form then names `cty: "application/vcon+gzip"`, the second value [section 5.3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-5.3.1) lists.
- Encrypted data does not compress, so a rule that wants a smaller file compresses before encryption.
- [Section 6.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-6.2) says applications SHOULD accept a gzip vCon and need not send one.
- `compress = "none"`, the default, writes the vCon uncompressed.
- sipnab writes no JWE `zip` header.

The file holds the JWE: `unprotected`, `recipients`, `iv`, `ciphertext` and
`tag`.

- Its `unprotected` header carries:
  - the container's `uuid`;
  - `enc: "A256CBC-HS512"`;
  - `cty: "application/vcon"`, or `application/vcon+gzip` with `compress = "gzip"`.
  - [core-04 section 5.3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-5.3.1) lists these.
  - A store and the forwarder's replace URL can use the uuid without the key.
- Each recipient's `header` carries `alg: "RSA-OAEP"`.
- With nothing left for a protected header to hold, the JWE has no `protected` member.
- sipnab 0.5.217 and 0.5.218 wrote `alg` and `enc` in a `protected` member, and `x5c` in the signature's protected header.
  - The fetcher reads those containers too.
- sipnab names each file `<uuid>.vcon.json` rather than after the Call-ID.
  - A Call-ID can carry host names and addresses, and the file name is not encrypted.

- Its `unprotected` header carries the container's
  `uuid` and `cty: "application/vcon+json"`.
  - So a store and the forwarder's replace URL can use the uuid without the key.
- sipnab names each file `<uuid>.vcon.json` rather than after the Call-ID.
  - A Call-ID can carry host names and addresses.
  - The file name is not encrypted.

**Decrypt one.**

- The recipient opens the container with the private key of
  the `encrypt_to` certificate.
- Then the recipient verifies the signature against the
  certificate in `x5c`.
- The working group's reference tool is the `vcon`
  command of [vcon-dev/vcon](https://github.com/vcon-dev/vcon).
  - It does this with `vcon decrypt <key> <cert>` and then `vcon verify <ca cert>`.
- sipnab's tests check its output against the draft's own encrypted example (Appendix A.7):
  - sipnab decrypts that example and verifies its signature.
  - It signs the same bytes with the same key to the same signature.

**What the keys must be.**

- `encrypt_to` and `sign_cert` hold PEM certificates. Each key is RSA, at
  least 2048 bits.
- `sign_key` is a PEM RSA private key (`PRIVATE KEY` or `RSA PRIVATE KEY`).
  It is readable by its owner only.
  - The first certificate in `sign_cert` must be that key's certificate.
- sipnab does not check who issued either certificate or when it expires.
  - Whoever decrypts a container decides whether to trust the signer's chain.
  - The fetcher checks it with `--vcon-fetch-signer-ca` and
    `--vcon-fetch-signer-sha256` (see [Check who signed it](#check-who-signed-it)).

**What it refuses at startup**, naming the rule:

- `encrypt_to` without `sign_key` and `sign_cert`, or either of those without
  `encrypt_to`
- a key or certificate file that sipnab cannot read, that holds no key or certificate,
  or that holds a key other than RSA of at least 2048 bits
- a `sign_cert` whose first certificate is not the certificate of `sign_key`
- a `sign_key` that other users can read (`chmod 600` it)
- `audio = "url"`: sipnab would not encrypt the WAV file beside the container.
  Use `inline` or `omit`.
- a `compress` other than `none` or `gzip`, or `compress` on a rule without
  `encrypt_to`

Every other rule key works with `encrypt_to`.

- A `live = true` rule writes a new encrypted container each time the call
  changes. [When an encrypted call changes](#when-an-encrypted-call-changes)
  says what that container is.
- Enrichment services receive the call before sipnab encrypts it, as without `encrypt_to`.

**Set the keys once for every rule.** `encrypt_to`, `sign_key`, `sign_cert`
and `compress` in the `[vcon]` section are the values of each rule that does
not set its own. A rule's own value overrides the section's, key by key:

```toml
[vcon]
encrypt_to = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-recipient.crt"
sign_key   = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-signing.key"
sign_cert  = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-signing.crt"
compress   = "gzip"

[[vcon.rule]]
name = "support"
when = "@support"
dir  = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"

[[vcon.rule]]
name       = "legal"
when       = "@legal"
dir        = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/legal"
encrypt_to = "/etc/sipnab/vcon-legal.crt"
compress   = "none"
```

Here both rules sign with the section's key. `support` encrypts to the
section's certificate with gzip, and `legal` to its own certificate without
it. A rule encrypts when it has an `encrypt_to`, its own or the section's, so
with `[vcon] encrypt_to` set every rule encrypts. The section's `sign_key`,
`sign_cert` and `compress` apply only to a rule that encrypts: without
`[vcon] encrypt_to`, a rule with no `encrypt_to` of its own writes the
unsigned form. The rule `--export-vcon-when` with `--export-vcon-dir` makes
takes none of them. sipnab refuses at startup a `[vcon] compress` other than
`none` or `gzip`. `sealed_updates` is not one of the section's keys: each rule
sets its own.

#### When an encrypted call changes

A rule rewrites a call's container when the call changes after sipnab wrote it.

- A `live = true` rule rewrites it on every change.
- Any other rule on a live capture rewrites it on a late change. A `BYE` after
  an idle write is one. A retransmitted final response is another.

[Section 4.1.9 of draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.1.9)
rules that out for a signed or encrypted container.

- A change invalidates the container.
- So the draft requires a new vCon instance version for each change.
- It says the new version SHOULD name the prior one by its uuid.
- A rule without `encrypt_to` writes the unsigned form. The draft lets a
  producer modify that form, so such a rule rewrites it in place.

`sealed_updates` sets what an encrypting rule does instead. A rule that does
not set it uses `new-uuid`, whether its `encrypt_to` is its own or the
section's.

| Value | What the rule writes |
|-------|----------------------|
| `new-uuid` (the default) | Each later version of the call is a new instance in a new file, `<uuid>.vcon.json`. Its `amended` object names the uuid of the version before it. It keeps the first version's `created_at`, and its `updated_at` is when sipnab wrote it. The earlier files stay |
| `same-uuid` | Each later version replaces the file under the same uuid, as releases before this setting did. This departs from section 4.1.9. It also departs from [section 4.1.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.1.2), which requires every uuid to be globally unique. sipnab logs one warning at startup naming the rule |
| `final-only` | Nothing while the call is in progress. One encrypted container once every leg has ended, and none after it. When the run ends during a call, sipnab writes that call once then, and its completeness block records `call_ended: false` |

sipnab refuses at startup any other `sealed_updates` value, naming the three.

**The uuid of a later version.**

- The first version has the call's uuid.
- The uuid of version *n* (1, 2 and so on) keeps the first uuid's 48-bit timestamp.
- It takes its other 74 bits from SHA-256 over `amended`, the first uuid and *n*.
- It depends on nothing else. So two runs over the same capture write the same
  chain of uuids.

To read a call's latest version, follow the chain. The latest version is the
one that no other version names in `amended`.

## The spool contract, for a bridge that consumes it

`--export-vcon-dir` is a queue, and it never runs alone.

- It pairs with `--export-vcon-when`. That flag names the dialogs to emit, in the same expression
  language `--filter` speaks.
- Each flag requires the other.
- `--export-vcon-when` conflicts with the single-call `--export-vcon`.
  - One writes a container per matching dialog.
  - The other writes exactly one.

```bash
sipnab -N -d eth0 --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir /var/spool/vcon
```

The capture process never sends a container anywhere.

- The export path writes files and makes no outbound connection.
- Delivering them to a store is the job of a separate process that watches the directory.
- sipnab includes one, `sipnab --vcon-forward`.
  [Deliver the spool to a store](#deliver-the-spool-to-a-store) describes it.
- Any other program can do the same job.

These are the guarantees a forwarder may rely on.

**When a container appears depends on where the calls come from.**

- On a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`), sipnab writes a matching call's
  container while it keeps capturing.
  - It checks every five seconds.
  - It writes a call once the call has ended and has been quiet for five seconds.
    Ended means Completed, Canceled, Failed, Redirected, Expired or Terminated.
  - Expect the container about ten seconds after the call's last message, at the latest.
  - The call can change after that. For example, a late `200 OK` answers a canceled
    call. sipnab then writes the container again under the same name.
- sipnab writes a call that has not ended once it has carried no SIP message
  and no RTP packet for 120 seconds.
  - This covers a call whose BYE sipnab never saw. For example, a phone lost power, or the capture point missed the
    packet.
  - Without it, sipnab would never write that call.
  - The container's `call_ended` field is `false`. Its completeness note says the call had not
    ended when sipnab wrote it (see
    [When the call had not ended](#when-the-call-had-not-ended)).
  - If the BYE, or any other message, arrives later, sipnab writes the container again under
    the same name.
  - A forwarder that already delivered the first copy may be
    refused the second by its store. For example, vcon.store answers `409` for
    a uuid it already holds.
  - sipnab writes a call on hold with no media for 120 seconds early, in the same way.
  - Idle compaction keeps a quiet call's opening request and outcome. It drops the messages between them.
    - It runs after `[limits] idle_compact_after_secs` (600 seconds by default).
    - So it does not reach a call before the live export writes it.
    - A live export run with that setting below 120 seconds warns at startup. Compaction could then
      drop a call's middle messages before sipnab writes its container.
- A live capture that you stop writes nothing more. Stop means `systemctl stop`, SIGTERM, Ctrl-C, or an MCP
  client that goes away.
  - sipnab does not write calls it had not yet written on the way out. Stopping sipnab must leave
    no call data behind.
- A live run can end on its own (`--duration`, `--autostop`).
  - It writes the matching calls the checks had not reached yet.
  - It does not write a second copy of any container already written.
  - Its last line counts both, for example `Wrote no further vCon containers to 'spool'
    at the end of the run; 1 container(s) were written there as their calls
    ended.`
- With `-I`, sipnab reads the whole capture and writes every container at the
  end, as before.

sipnab refuses some flags on a live capture:

- `--redact`, `--redact-map` and `--content-deny-tombstone` with `--export-vcon-when`,
- `--redact` and `--redact-map` with `--export-vcon`.

These flags write their files at the end of the run. A stopped live run never gets there. Use them with `-I`.

**A name resolves to a whole container, or to nothing.** Every write:

- stages the bytes under a dot-prefixed sibling,
- flushes them to the filesystem,
- renames into place.

So a reader polling the directory never sees a truncated
container. A write that fails leaves the previous one intact.

Staging is deliberately in the DESTINATION directory rather than in the system temp dir:

- `rename` is atomic only within one filesystem.
- Across a mount boundary, it either fails outright or degrades into a copy.
- A copy puts the partial file back.

**A staging file you can see is litter.**

- sipnab writes it as `.<container>.partial`. So an ordinary listing and a `*.json` glob both skip
  it.
- A failed write removes it.
- One left behind means sipnab died mid-write. It is safe to delete.

**Names are stable, and sipnab reuses them.** A container's file name comes
from its Call-ID:

- An underscore replaces every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`.
- An underscore also replaces a leading dot. So no container name starts with one.
- The name ends in a hyphen, 16 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 of the Call-ID,
  and `.vcon.json`. An example is `1-1966_10.0.2.20-1cc03f180ff8a774.vcon.json`.
- Re-exporting the same dialog to the same directory overwrites its file.
  - It does not accumulate a second one.
  - That is what makes the directory a queue and not a log.

Two dialogs can have Call-IDs that differ only outside that character set, or only
beyond the first 180 characters. They still get two names:

- The readable part of the name can match.
- The SHA-256 suffix differs.

**With `--redact`, the name comes from the redacted Call-ID.**

- sipnab names the file after the pseudonym the container carries in `sip_call_id`.
- So the original Call-ID and the host address inside it appear in none of these:
  - the spool,
  - the `--vcon-digest` lines,
  - the forwarder's `delivered/` and `failed/` directories and log lines.
- The name still matches the Call-ID inside the container.
- With the same `--redact-key-file`, a re-export produces the same
  name and overwrites the file.

**A container is complete when it appears.** There is no partial state, no
lock file and no sentinel to wait for. Read it, forward it, delete it.

**Deleting is the consumer's job.** sipnab never removes a container it wrote.
So a spool nobody drains grows without bound.

**`--vcon-digest` gives you something to reconcile against.**

- It prints a SHA-256 of every container written, in `sha256sum` format.
- So `sipnab ... --vcon-digest > SHA256SUMS` and a later `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`
  both work with no glue.
- It is deliberately not a signature, and deliberately outside the container.
  - A store adds fields on ingest.
  - So a signature over sipnab's bytes would fail against the object the store holds.
  - It would tell an operator nothing.

## Deliver the spool to a store

`sipnab --vcon-forward` is a second sipnab process, started on its own.

- It delivers the containers in an `--export-vcon-dir` spool to a vCon store over
  HTTP or HTTPS.
- It needs the `vcon` feature, like the export.
- It captures nothing. sipnab refuses `--vcon-forward` beside any of these:
  - `-d`, `-I`, `--hep-listen`,
  - a capture filter,
  - a listener,
  - an export flag.
- So the capture process keeps making no outbound connection.

Captures carry personal data, and a store belongs to another party. Decide
what may leave the machine before you forward anything:

- `--redact` on the export replaces identities and addresses with keyed tokens.
- [What may you conclude](#someone-handed-you-a-sipnab-vcon-what-may-you-conclude)
  lists what a container carries.

### Run it

The forwarder needs two things:

- where the store is,
- the credential that authenticates you.

Give the store's URL once, in a shell variable. Put the
one header that authenticates you in a file that only you can read.

- The forwarder refuses the file when your group or other users can read it.
  This is the same rule sipnab applies to its other secret files.
- The file holds one line, `Header-Name: value`:

```sh
# Run all of these, in order.
STORE_URL='http://127.0.0.1:8000/vcon/external-ingress?ingress_list=sipnab'
umask 077
printf 'x-conserver-api-token: %s\n' "$KEY" > vcon-forward.auth
sipnab --vcon-forward ./spool --vcon-forward-url "$STORE_URL" \
  --vcon-forward-auth-file vcon-forward.auth --vcon-forward-once
echo "exit $?"
```

`$KEY` is the key the store gave you.

- For a store that takes a bearer token, the line is `Authorization: Bearer <token>` instead.
- The value never appears in a log line, an error message or a failure record.
- The forwarder removes it from any store answer it keeps, even one that echoes the request back.

The credential can come from the environment instead of a file.

- `SIPNAB_VCON_FORWARD_AUTH` holds exactly what the file would hold.
- The `--vcon-forward-auth` flag takes the same value.
  - But a flag's value is visible in the process list to other users of the host.
  - So prefer the variable or the file.
- The credential has one source.
  - sipnab refuses the variable or the flag beside `--vcon-forward-auth-file` or `[vcon_forward] auth_file`.
  - It refuses an empty one.
- A capture run ignores the variable.

```sh
# Run all of these, in order.
export SIPNAB_VCON_FORWARD_AUTH="x-conserver-api-token: $KEY"
sipnab --vcon-forward ./spool --vcon-forward-url "$STORE_URL" --vcon-forward-once
```

`--vcon-forward-once` makes one pass and exits. The exit codes are:

- `0` when the store accepted every container, or the spool held none,
- `1` when the store refused one, or one is still waiting,
- `2` when sipnab refuses a setting given on the command line,
- `3` when the store refused the credentials or the client.

Some configuration errors exit differently:

- A config file sipnab refuses exits `1`, as on any run.
- So does an `[vcon_forward]
  auth_file` that sipnab cannot read or that holds no credential.
- The same file named by `--vcon-forward-auth-file` exits `2`.

Without `--vcon-forward-once`, the forwarder makes a pass every
`--vcon-forward-interval` seconds (default 5) until SIGTERM or SIGINT.

- Stopping it means stopping. It sends nothing more after the signal.
- A container it had not reached stays in the spool for the next run.

### Choose the store kind

Stores differ in three ways:

- where they take a container,
- how they authenticate,
- what they answer for a uuid they hold.

`--vcon-forward-kind` (or `[vcon_forward] kind`) names the kind of store.

- The kind supplies those values.
- So you give the store's base URL and the bare key:

| Kind | Ingest path added to a base URL | The header a bare key goes in | A uuid it holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generic` (default) | none: the URL is the endpoint | not accepted: give `Header-Name: value` | not measured |
| `vcon-store` | `/v1/vcons` | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | `500`, which the forwarder retries like any `5xx` |
| `conserver` | `/vcon/external-ingress?ingress_list=sipnab` | `x-conserver-api-token: <key>` | `204`, and the store replaces its copy |

No kind changes the container sent. Each value is what the store did when
measured:

- vcon.store on 2026-10-09, in
  [Send sipnab's vCons to vcon.store](@/docs/vcon-store.md#the-measurements).
- conserver on 2026-10-07. This is a self-hosted vCon server. It received a synthetic container from sipnab's test
  fixtures.
  - It answered `204` for a new container. `GET /vcon/{uuid}` then
    returned the container with an `amended` member added.
  - It answered `204` for the same uuid sent again. The read-back then showed the second copy.
  - It answered `422` for a body that is not JSON, and for one without `uuid`.
  - It answered `403` with no key or a wrong one.

Every kind counts any `2xx` as delivered. The
`sipnab` ingress list is the one that
[Run sipnab with a vCon server](@/docs/vcon-sipnab.md) creates.

An explicit setting overrides each value the kind supplies:

- A URL that names a path is the endpoint as written.
  - The kind adds its path only to a URL with none (`https://api.vcon.store`, not
    `https://api.vcon.store/v1/vcons`).
- The forwarder sends a credential that is a full `Header-Name: value` line as
  written.
  - The kind forms the header only from a bare key.
  - So give a key that itself holds a colon as the full line.
- `--vcon-forward-replace-url` applies to any kind.
  - No kind sets one. Nobody has measured a `PUT` to vcon.store.

```sh
# Run all of these, in order.
STORE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000
umask 077
printf '%s\n' "$KEY" > conserver.key
sipnab --vcon-forward ./spool --vcon-forward-kind conserver \
  --vcon-forward-url "$STORE_URL" --vcon-forward-auth-file conserver.key \
  --vcon-forward-once
```

### Keep the settings in sipnab.toml

Every forwarder flag has a key in the `[vcon_forward]` section of the
[config file](@/docs/config.md#vcon-forward). The exceptions are `--vcon-forward`, `--vcon-forward-once` and
`--vcon-forward-auth`.

- A flag overrides its key.
- So a file holds the standing settings, and a command line changes one for one run:

```toml
[vcon_forward]
kind = "conserver"
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
auth_file = "/etc/sipnab/conserver.key"
done = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon-sent"
failed = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon-held"
interval = 5
```

```sh
sipnab --vcon-forward /var/spool/sipnab-vcon --config /etc/sipnab/vcon-forward.toml
```

sipnab checks each key by the rule its flag follows.

- Some errors stop any run that loads the file:
  - a number out of range,
  - an unknown kind,
  - a first back-off longer than the cap.
- A URL or a credential the forwarder cannot use stops the
  forwarder at startup. The message names the key.

### Deliver to two stores

One forwarder delivers to one store.

- It moves each container out of the spool once the store accepts it.
- So two forwarders cannot share one spool. The
  first would take every container from the second.

To deliver to two stores, chain them:

- The second forwarder's spool is the first one's delivered directory.
- Each has its own delivered directory.
- Run each as a process of its own, in two terminals or as two services.

The first delivers to a conserver:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-forward ./spool --vcon-forward-kind conserver \
  --vcon-forward-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --vcon-forward-auth-file conserver.key \
  --vcon-forward-done ./spool/delivered
```

The second delivers what the first delivered to vcon.store:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-forward ./spool/delivered --vcon-forward-kind vcon-store \
  --vcon-forward-url https://api.vcon.store --vcon-forward-auth-file vcon-store.key \
  --vcon-forward-done ./spool/delivered/vcon-store
```

A container reaches the second store only after the first accepted it.

- A container the first refused stays in the first one's failed directory.
- It never reaches the second.

### What it does with each container

The forwarder POSTs the file's bytes unchanged. It sends these headers:

- `Content-Type: application/json`,
- `User-Agent: sipnab/<version>`,
- the header from the file.

Then it moves the file by the answer:

| The store answers | The forwarder |
|---|---|
| `2xx` | moves the file to `--vcon-forward-done`, `delivered/` in the spool by default, under its own name, and logs a `delivered` line |
| `401` or `403` | stops. The answer refuses the credentials or the client, so every container would draw it: the forwarder sends nothing more, moves no file, logs one error line naming the status and the first 200 bytes of the answer, and exits `3`, with or without `--vcon-forward-once` |
| `409`, with `--vcon-forward-replace-url` | PUTs the same bytes to that URL, with `{uuid}` replaced by the container's `uuid`, and acts on that answer |
| any other `4xx`, `409` included without a replace URL | moves the file to `--vcon-forward-failed`, `failed/` in the spool by default, beside `<name>.error.json`, and logs one line naming the file and the status |
| `5xx`, a timeout, or no connection | leaves the file in the spool and tries it again after `--vcon-forward-backoff-first` seconds (default 2), then twice that, and so on up to `--vcon-forward-backoff-cap` seconds (default 300). The other containers are not held up |

`<name>.error.json` holds:

- the status,
- the method and URL,
- the first `--vcon-forward-max-error-body` bytes (default 8192) of the store's answer.

Some answers count as no answer:

- An answer whose status line and headers exceed `--vcon-forward-max-response-head`
  bytes (default 65536) counts as no answer.
- The container then waits for a retry.

The delivered and failed directories must be on the
spool's file system. That way, every move is a rename.

To see the spool's state, use any of these:

- run `sipnab --vcon-spool-status <SPOOL_DIR>`,
- call [`vcon_spool_status`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md#vcon-spool-status) on the capture's MCP
  server,
- read [`GET /v1/vcon/spool`](@/docs/api.md#get-v1-vcon-spool) from its
  REST server.

All three give one answer.

- It counts the containers pending in the spool and in the default
  `delivered/` and `failed/` directories.
- It returns each failed container's `<name>.error.json` record.
- It reads files and nothing else.
- The answer is a snapshot dated by its `as_of` field. The forwarder may move a file a moment
  later.

The forwarder reads the spool by the contract above.

- It skips dot-prefixed names and names that do not end in `.json`. So it never reads a staging file.
- sipnab can rewrite a container under the same name because the call changed.
  - The rewritten file is a new container to the forwarder, and it goes out again.
  - That holds when the rewrite lands after delivery.
  - It also holds when the rewrite lands while the send is in flight.
  - The forwarder checks that the file it moves is the file it
    sent. It leaves a newer one in the spool for the next pass.

### Trust a store's certificate

Over `https://`, the forwarder and the fetcher verify the store's
certificate against the host's CA bundle. Two settings change that, the same
pair the HEP sender has (`--hep-tls-ca` and `--hep-tls-extra-ca`):

| Forwarder | Fetcher | What the client trusts |
|-----------|---------|------------------------|
| -- | -- | the host's CA bundle |
| `--vcon-forward-ca <FILE>` | `--vcon-fetch-ca <FILE>` | only the CA certificates in the file |
| `--vcon-forward-extra-ca <FILE>` | `--vcon-fetch-extra-ca <FILE>` | the host's CA bundle and the CA certificates in the file |

Use the second form for a store whose certificate a private CA issued, on a
host whose public roots should still count. sipnab refuses the two together,
and refuses the second form on a host with no CA bundle to add to. In the
config file the keys are `ca` and `extra_ca` in `[vcon_forward]` and
`[vcon_fetch]`. A flag of either form replaces both keys of its section.

### What it guarantees, and what it does not

- **A `2xx` means the store accepted the container, not that it kept it.**
  - The forwarder logs `delivered`, never `stored`.
  - A self-hosted conserver once answered `204` for a container it then failed to write.
    Nothing in the answer said so.
  - To know the store kept a container, look in the store.
- **The bytes are sipnab's.** The forwarder never changes a container. It
  sends the file's bytes, whatever the kind.
- **It does not retry a refusal.**
  - This covers a `4xx` other than a `401`, a `403` or a `409` it can replace.
  - That container stays in the failed directory until a person reads the
    record and decides.
- **A refused credential stops it, and moves nothing.**
  - A wrong key draws a `401` or `403` for every container.
  - So the forwarder stops at the first one and leaves the whole spool where it is.
  - The log line quotes the start of the answer. For example, a Cloudflare front that refuses the client answers `403` with
    `error code: 1010`.
  - Fix the credential or the client, and start the forwarder again.
- **It does not delete anything.**
  - The delivered directory keeps a copy of every container. Every copy is call data.
  - Delete them on a schedule that suits you.
- **It adds no signature and no consent.**
  - It sends each container as the rule wrote it.
  - A store may sign what it receives. That signature is the
    store's, over an observation.
  - sipnab records no consent.
- **It sends one container at a time**, in name order, one connection each.

## Fetch a stored vCon

`sipnab --vcon-fetch` is the forwarder's counterpart.

- It is a separate sipnab process.
- It reads containers back from a store by uuid, and writes each to a file.
- It needs the `vcon` feature.
- Like the forwarder, it captures nothing.
  - sipnab refuses it beside any capture source, listener or export flag.
  - So the capture process keeps making no outbound connection.

### Fetch one

Give the store's base URL, its kind, and a file holding the key. The file is readable only
by you. The fetcher writes each container to `<uuid>.vcon.json` in
`--vcon-fetch-out`:

```sh
# Run all of these, in order.
umask 077
printf '%s\n' "$KEY" > conserver.key
sipnab --vcon-fetch 018bcfe5-6800-8a6b-a667-78f1c5213800 \
  --vcon-fetch-kind conserver --vcon-fetch-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --vcon-fetch-auth-file conserver.key --vcon-fetch-out fetched
echo "exit $?"
```

`$KEY` is the key the store gave you. Give several uuids after `--vcon-fetch`.
Or give `-` to read them from standard input, one per line:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-fetch - --vcon-fetch-kind conserver --vcon-fetch-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --vcon-fetch-auth-file conserver.key --vcon-fetch-out fetched < uuids.txt
```

Each fetcher flag has a key in the `[vcon_fetch]` section of the
[config file](@/docs/config.md#vcon-fetch). The flag overrides the key. The exceptions are `--vcon-fetch`, `--vcon-fetch-out` and
`--vcon-fetch-overwrite`. The
[CLI reference](@/docs/cli.md#vcon-fetcher) lists every flag.

### The store kinds

| Kind | Read path added after the path in the URL | The header a bare key goes in | What the store wraps around the container |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generic` (default) | none: the URL is a template holding `{uuid}` | not accepted: give `Header-Name: value` | nothing |
| `vcon-store` | `/v1/vcons/{uuid}` | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | a top-level `_meta` member, which the fetcher removes |
| `conserver` | `/vcon/{uuid}` | `x-conserver-api-token: <key>` | nothing |
| `vcon-mcp` | `/api/v1/vcons/{uuid}` | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | `{"success": true, "vcon": {...}}`; the fetcher keeps the `vcon` member |

Sources:

- vcon.store: its OpenAPI document, and a `GET` on 2026-10-09 that returned
  the container's members and `_meta`.
- conserver: `api/api.py` of the vCon server (`vcon-dev/vcon-server`).
- vcon-mcp: `src/api/routes/vcons.ts`, `src/api/rest-router.ts` and
  `src/api/auth.ts` of `vcon-dev/vcon-mcp`.

A URL that names a path keeps it. The kind's read path follows it.

- For example, for a conserver served under `/api`, give `--vcon-fetch-url http://127.0.0.1:8000/api`.
- The fetcher takes a URL holding `{uuid}` as written, for any kind.

### What it does with each answer

| The store answers | The fetcher |
|---|---|
| `2xx` with the container | writes it to `<uuid>.vcon.json`, mode `0600`, without the kind's envelope, every other byte as the store sent it. With `--vcon-fetch-decrypt-key`, it writes an encrypted container decrypted: see [Fetch an encrypted vCon](#fetch-an-encrypted-vcon) |
| `2xx` with a body larger than `--vcon-fetch-max-size`, not JSON, without the kind's envelope, or holding another uuid | writes nothing for that uuid |
| `404` | writes nothing for that uuid, and logs that the store holds none |
| `401` or `403` | stops: asks for no further uuid, and exits `3` |
| another status, a timeout or no connection | writes nothing for that uuid, logs the status and the start of the answer with the credential removed, and goes on to the next uuid. It does not retry |

The fetcher checks each container it writes against the vendored vCon schema.

- A container the schema refuses is still written, as the store holds it.
  - It is the store's record. You need it to see what is wrong.
- The log line lists each finding, and the run exits `1`.

A file that already exists is not replaced.

- The fetcher does not ask the store for that uuid, and the run exits `1`.
- `--vcon-fetch-overwrite` replaces it.
- Neither form writes through a symbolic link.

Exit codes:

- `0` when the fetcher wrote every container and the schema accepts
  each,
- `1` when it wrote none for some uuid, or the schema refuses one,
- `2` when sipnab refuses a setting given on the command line,
- `3` when the store refused the credential or the client.

A config file sipnab refuses exits `1`, as on any
run.

### Fetch an encrypted vCon

A container that an [encrypting rule](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes) wrote is in
the encrypted form, and a store hands it back as the forwarder sent it. Give the
fetcher the private key of the `encrypt_to` certificate, readable by its owner
only, and it writes the vCon inside:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-fetch 0158a120-0392-81a5-a0a3-98c35ae1193c \
  --vcon-fetch-kind conserver --vcon-fetch-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --vcon-fetch-auth-file conserver.key --vcon-fetch-out fetched \
  --vcon-fetch-decrypt-key /etc/sipnab/vcon-recipient.key
```

For each encrypted container the fetcher:

- finds the uuid in the container's `unprotected` header;
- decrypts it with the key;
- verifies the signature of the signed form inside against the first
  certificate in its `x5c`;
- inflates the payload when it is gzip (it starts with the gzip magic bytes
  `1f 8b`), stopping at `--vcon-fetch-max-size` bytes;
- checks that the vCon inside holds the uuid asked for;
- checks it against the vendored schema;
- writes it to `<uuid>.vcon.json`, mode `0600`.

The log line gives the SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate the signature
verified against. Compare it with your signing certificate:
`openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 -in vcon-signing.crt`.

If the key does not decrypt the container, the signature does not verify,
a header carries a JWE `zip`, or a gzip payload inflates past
`--vcon-fetch-max-size`, the fetcher writes nothing for that uuid and the run exits `1`. Without
`--vcon-fetch-decrypt-key`, it writes an encrypted container as the store
holds it, and says so in its log line.

#### Check who signed it

A valid signature shows that the holder of the key in `x5c` signed the
container. It does not show who that is. Two settings make the fetcher check
the signer before it writes anything. Each needs `--vcon-fetch-decrypt-key`.

- `--vcon-fetch-signer-ca <FILE>` (`[vcon_fetch] signer_ca`): the signing
  certificate must chain, through the intermediate certificates the
  container carries in `x5c`, to a CA certificate in this PEM file, and every
  certificate in that chain must be within its validity period now. The value
  `system` uses the host's CA bundle, the one the fetcher trusts for HTTPS;
  write `./system` for a file of that name. The fetcher does not check the
  signing certificate's extended key usage.
- `--vcon-fetch-signer-sha256 <HEX>` (`[vcon_fetch] signer_sha256`): the
  signing certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint must be this one. Write it as
  `openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256` prints it, or as 64 hex digits
  without colons, in either case.

```sh
sipnab --vcon-fetch 0158a120-0392-81a5-a0a3-98c35ae1193c \
  --vcon-fetch-kind conserver --vcon-fetch-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --vcon-fetch-auth-file conserver.key --vcon-fetch-out fetched \
  --vcon-fetch-decrypt-key /etc/sipnab/vcon-recipient.key \
  --vcon-fetch-signer-ca /etc/sipnab/vcon-signing-ca.pem
```

With both, the fetcher applies both. With either, it writes nothing for a
container whose signer fails the check, nor for a container that is not
encrypted, which has no signer to check. The log line says why and the run
exits `1`. When a container carries more than one signature, the checks
apply to the first, the one the log line names.

### Read what came back

Each file is one vCon, as JSON.

- `-I` reads it the way it reads a capture.
  For example: `sipnab -N -I fetched/<uuid>.vcon.json --analyze` (see
  [Analyze a stored vCon](#analyze-a-stored-vcon)).
- Any JSON tool reads it too.
  For example: `jq '.parties, .dialog[].type' fetched/<uuid>.vcon.json`.

## Walk through one, end to end

The capture is [`tests/fixtures/sip_call.pcap`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/tests/fixtures/sip_call.pcap).
This repository holds it as a committed file.

- It holds one INVITE, a 100, a 180, a 200, the ACK, a BYE
  and its 200.
- That is seven messages, one Call-ID, two parties.

### Check the build carries the feature

The committed integration test drives the whole export through the public API
against that capture. So running it confirms both the feature and the fixture
in one command:

```sh
cargo test --features vcon --test vcon_export_test
```

```text
running 2 tests
test a_real_capture_exports_a_complete_signaling_only_container ... ok
test re_exporting_one_dialog_from_one_capture_keeps_its_identifier ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.01s
```

### Build the container

The shortest path is the committed example. It does everything below against
that same capture, and it prints the container:

```sh
cargo run --features vcon --example export_vcon -- tests/fixtures/sip_call.pcap
```

Its source is [`examples/export_vcon.rs`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/examples/export_vcon.rs).

- It compiles as part of the build.
- So it cannot drift from the API the way a fragment on a page can.

In your own program:

- Read the capture into a `DialogStore` the ordinary way.
  The [library page](@/docs/library.md) covers that part.
- Then hand one dialog and the run's own counters to `export_dialog`:

```rust
use sipnab::analysis::CaptureFacts;
use sipnab::output::vcon::{ExportContext, export_dialog};

let dialog = store.get(&call_id).expect("the dialog is in the store");
let vcon = export_dialog(
    dialog,
    &ExportContext {
        // Derive this from the capture's CONTENT — a file name, a frame
        // digest. Never from a per-process identifier: the container's uuid
        // hashes this value, so a rotating one mints a fresh uuid every time
        // you reopen the same file.
        capture_id: "sip_call.pcap",
        // What the RUN saw outside this one dialog: frames read, SIP a port
        // gate discarded, dialogs the store rotated away.
        facts: &facts,
        // The ranked capture analysis, when the run did one. `None` is an
        // honest answer, and the container reports it as one rather than as
        // a clean bill.
        analysis: None,
        // `None` takes the default inline-media budget.
        max_inline_media_bytes: None,
        // The dialog's RTP quality, for the report's `media_quality`:
        // `sipnab::output::vcon::media_quality_for(&streams, &call_id)` builds
        // it from a `StreamStore`. Empty leaves the key out.
        media: &[],
    },
);
println!("{}", vcon.to_json().expect("the container serializes"));
```

### Read what came out

This is real output from that fixture. The page elides it only where the message trace repeats
itself. Every value below came off a run against the committed capture.

**One reading convention, stated once.** Every attachment and analysis `body`
below declares `"encoding": "json"`.

- [Section 2.3.2 of the core draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-2.3.2)
  defines that encoding as "The value of the body parameter is a JSON value
  (object, array, number, string, or one of the literals true, false, or null)".
- sipnab writes each of these bodies as the JSON object itself. A consumer
  indexes into it directly.
- A recording's body is `base64url` text, which is a string.
- A store can return a `json` body as a string holding the JSON text. sipnab's
  own readers accept both shapes.
