Four things in that output repay a second look.

**Three parties for a two-party call.** The last entry is sipnab.

- It carries no `sip` URI. sipnab sent no SIP, and a synthesized one would name a
  participant that never existed.
- Its `role` says `observer`.
- Both attachments point their `party` index at it (index 2).
  So every document in the container has a stated origin.

**The callee has fewer fields than the caller.** Party 1 carries a `sip` and
nothing else.

- sipnab reads a party's `Contact` and `User-Agent` off a message
  that party sent.
- In this capture, the first message coming back is a bare
  `100 Trying`. It carries neither.
- An absent field means the capture never saw
  one. It does not mean the endpoint has none.

**The Dialog Object describes no media, and that is correct here.**

- This run retained no RTP payload. So there is nothing to describe.
- Inventing a `mediatype` or a `url` would name a file that does not exist.
- The object's type is `recording` with no content. This is the placeholder of the type rule below.
- It has no `disposition`. The call in this fixture completed, and
  nothing about it failed.

**The completeness body appears twice.** It appears once as an attachment, and once inside the
report. The next section is about why.

## The container cannot say "this is an incomplete record", so sipnab says it twice

This is the point of the page.

sipnab's central discipline is reporting what it understood rather than what
the wire held.

- Its ranked problem list puts incompleteness findings *in* the
  list at `Severity::Blind`, above every call fault.
- So a capture that failed to decode or hit a retention cap can never render as clean.

**vCon has no field for that.** Not a weak one: none.

- The `type` enum admits five values and no others: `recording`, `recording-set`, `text`, `transfer`,
  `incomplete`.
- Four of the five promise content the object holds.
- The fifth names a call that "failed to be setup". That is a claim about the conversation rather
  than about the object.

So sipnab types the object by **what it carries**. It also uses the one outcome it
can observe, a final failure:
| The object holds | `type` | `disposition` |
|---|---|---|
| audio | `recording` | absent — it is an `incomplete` field |
| no content, no observed failure | `recording`, with no content | absent |
| no content, an observed final failure | `incomplete` | the reason, always |

The middle row is the placeholder of
[section 4.3 of the core draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.3).

- It is for a dialog the producer knows occurred but holds little or nothing from.
- Such a Dialog Object "contains only
  the type parameter". For a call that reached setup, its type is `recording`.
- [Section 4.3.8](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.3.8) waives `mediatype` when the content is
  absent.
- "No observed failure" covers:
  - an answered call,
  - a call whose final response the capture never saw,
  - a redirect.
- sipnab cannot tell from the wire whether the second reached setup. It does not report a failure it did
  not see.

Reaching for `incomplete` in that row is the mistake sipnab shipped until
0.5.128.

- It is not a matter of taste.
- It made every container for a call that answered assert a setup failure that never happened.

**Changed in this release, for draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04.**

- Until now, that row had no `type` at all. `draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-03` allowed "a
  Dialog Object with no parameters in it".
- `-04` removed that sentence. It requires `type` on every Dialog Object.
- So a container for a call with no media now carries `"type": "recording"` and no `body` or `url`.
- A consumer that selects `type == "recording"` and then reads the content must check that the
  content is there.
- Measured in the vcon-server conserver source at commit `8ffbfcf`:
  - The `deepgram_link` transcription link reads `dialog["url"]` with a
    bracket, and raises on such an object.
  - The `hugging_face_whisper` and `groq_whisper` links read `dialog["duration"]` the same way.
  - The type-free object raised in all four transcription links, `openai_transcribe` included,
    at `dialog["type"]`.

The last two rows move together.

- [Section 4.3.11 of the core draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.3.11) makes `disposition` a MUST
  on an incomplete object.
- No value in its closed set means "not observed".
- So one decision fixes both fields.
- `disposition` names a failure **only** when sipnab saw the final response that caused it.
- Its absence never means "the call succeeded".

sipnab maps the final response to a value of that closed set:

| Final response | `disposition` | What section 4.3.11 defines the value as |
|---|---|---|
| `486`, `600` | `busy` | the party was busy with another conversation |
| `503` | `congestion` | system load stopped the attempt from completing |
| `408`, `480`, and `487` after a CANCEL sipnab saw | `no-answer` | nobody answered or accepted the attempt |
| any other `4xx`, `5xx` or `6xx`, a `487` with no CANCEL in the capture included | `failed` | the attempt failed, the value for a reason sipnab does not know |

A caller who gives up while the call rings sends CANCEL.

- The call ends with `487 Request Terminated`.
- Nobody answered, so that call is `no-answer`.
- sipnab never writes `hung-up`. The section defines it for a call that
  connected and then ended before any conversation.
- An answered call is not an `incomplete` object. The section says
  `disposition` "SHOULD NOT be present for other dialog types".

The extension mechanism offers no repair either. An extension is one of two kinds:

- *ignorable*: the consumer that most needs the caveat drops it,
- *fatal*: an ordinary consumer refuses the whole container.

Nothing in between means "read this before trusting the contents".

So sipnab duplicates the caveat into two surfaces a consumer walks past. Both come from
one source value:

| Surface | Where it sits | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `capture_completeness`, inside `analysis[0].body` | inside the report, beside the diagnosis | anything that reads what sipnab concluded |
| the `sipnab-capture-completeness` attachment | a document in `attachments`, attributed to the observer | anything that walks the attachments |

Both hold the same value byte for byte. A test fails if they diverge.

- Two caveats that disagreed would read as authoritative while contradicting
  themselves.
- That is worse than carrying none.

### What the caveat looks like when the run lost something

This is the same capture and the same dialog. The run's parser rejected three frames. Its
idle compaction discarded four messages it had already captured:

```json
{
  "purpose": "sipnab-capture-completeness",
  "party": 2,
  "mediatype": "application/json",
  "encoding": "json",
  "body": {
    "dialogs_refused": 0,
    "dialogs_rotated": 0,
    "frames_read": 22,
    "messages_evicted": 4,
    "node": "capture-01",
    "note": "Produced by sipnab 0.5.127 on node capture-01. … sipnab read 22 frame(s) for this capture. — INCOMPLETE: 3 frame(s) reached the parser and produced nothing, so any count in this container is a floor. — INCOMPLETE: idle compaction discarded 4 message(s) sipnab had already captured, so the trace in this container may be shorter than the call was. Raise [limits] keep_messages_per_idle_dialog to hold more. No capture-level analysis was supplied for this export, so nothing here rules out a blind spot.",
    "sip_discarded_by_port_gate": 0,
    "sip_discarded_by_websocket_gate": 0,
    "sipnab_version": "0.5.124",
    "undecodable_frames": 3
  }
}
```

Elided at the `…` only. The fixed preamble is identical to the clean run's.

Read the shape rather than the wording.

- Every clause is a **measurement** of this run.
- None of them says the call was short, silent or broken.
  None of that follows from a capture that missed something.
- `messages_evicted:
  4` and the sentence naming it move together. So a consumer that reads fields
  reaches the same verdict as one that reads prose.

Note the last clause in both runs: no capture analysis reached this export, so
the note says so.

- "Nobody checked" and "checked and found nothing" are different answers.
- The container keeps them apart:
  - an analysis that ranked nothing emits `blind_spots: []`,
  - an export that skipped the analysis omits the field entirely.

### When the call had not ended

`call_ended` is `true` when sipnab had seen the call's closing message before it wrote the container.
That message is the BYE, CANCEL or final failure response that closes the call.

It is `false` for:

- a call still running at the end of a `-I` capture,
- a call a live export wrote after 120 seconds with no SIP and no RTP.

When it is `false`, the note adds this sentence:

```text
The call had not ended when this container was written: sipnab had seen no BYE, CANCEL or final failure for it, so the trace and any media end where this container was written, not where the call ended.
```

This is a statement about the call, not about the capture.

- So it is not an `INCOMPLETE` clause. It adds no entry to the omission rows.
- Every message sipnab held can be in the container while the call continued after sipnab
  wrote it.
- The field is always present, including as `true`.

### When a container is missing on purpose

Two of the fields in that block report a **decision** rather than a capture
fault. The note says so in words.

- Every other clause describes something the run failed to see.
- These two describe something an operator chose.
- A reader who cannot tell them apart goes looking for a fault that does not exist.

| Field | What it means |
|---|---|
| `gate_closed_during_run` | An operator stopped this run writing content partway through, over `POST /v1/persistence`. Containers are absent on one side of a hole this capture does not otherwise record. |
| `dialogs_suppressed_by_deny` | How many dialogs carried the `--content-deny-header` name and produced no container. |

`--content-deny-header` suppresses the whole dialog, not merely its content.

- The default is the conservative reading: a denied dialog leaves this process
  entirely.
  - The REST route `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` answers `403` for it.
  - MCP `export_vcon` refuses it by `call_id`.
    It leaves it out of a filtered export, counting it in `withheld_by_deny`.
- `--content-deny-tombstone` makes the narrower reading available.
  - That is an identity-only container carrying a `redacted` object
    ([section 4.1.8 of the core draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.1.8)).
  - It has no message trace, no media and no bodies.
  - The trade is explicit, because a tombstone reveals that the call existed.
  - Leave it off when the header means "this call must leave no trace".

Both are always present, including as `false` and `0`.

- A missing key and "nothing happened" are the same fact here.
- There is no reason to make a consumer distinguish them.

The absence is what makes them necessary.

- A container written after recording stopped looks exactly like one from a run where those calls never happened.
  - So a reader comparing the set against a switch's records concludes sipnab missed
    them.
- The same goes for a deny flag. The containers that DID get written read
  as the complete set for their predicate.
- Neither fact survives in the capture itself. So the container carries it.

Suppression narrows and never widens.

- A header asking sipnab to RECORD is an assertion by whoever sent the request.
- This tool refuses that class of claim.
  - There is no permit flag.
  - No REST call can enable persistence a command line did not authorize.
- See [`docs/rest-api.md`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/rest-api.md)
  for the runtime gate.

## Someone handed you a sipnab vCon — what may you conclude?

Read the container as evidence from an instrument. Do not read it as a record from a
participant.

| What you see | What it licenses you to say | What it does not |
|---|---|---|
| `parties[].sip` | the `From` or `To` header carried this URI | that anyone with that URI took part |
| `parties[].sip_display_name` | the sender wrote this string in its header | that this names a person |
| `parties[].sip_user_agent` and `parties[].sip_contact` | a message this party sent carried the `User-Agent` or `Server` and `Contact` header: for the caller, the opening request; for the callee, a response from 101 to 699 carrying the dialog's remote `To` tag, or a request carrying it as the `From` tag. A proxy's `100 Trying` and any response without that tag are never read for the callee | that the software named is what the party runs |
| `validation: "none"` on every party | nobody checked anything about this party | that a check failed — the field never carries another value |
| a `role: "observer"` party | this container came from a tap | that the tap was in the media path |
| `attachments[].party` | the observer contributed this document | that a participant did |
| the message trace | these messages reached sipnab's parser | that they are all the messages |
| `analysis[0].body` | sipnab's diagnosis of what it held | a diagnosis of the call |
| `analysis[0].body.media_quality` | each RTP stream's MOS and R-factor, computed from the packets sipnab read, with `mos_grounded` saying whether the MOS rests on a published impairment value | that a listener heard that quality |
| an absent field | the capture did not carry it | that the call lacked it |
| a `dialog[]` object with no media fields | this export carries no media | that the call had none |
| `parties` on a `recording` with a `body` | the stream on each channel came from the address and port the named party advertised in its own SDP | that the party spoke, or that the channel holds only that party's audio |
| a `recording` with a `body` and no `parties` | at least one channel came from an address and port no party advertised in its SDP, such as a media relay's | that nobody was on that channel |

Three rules follow from that table.

**A missing thing is a missing observation.**

- Every absence in a sipnab vCon describes the capture. It never describes the conversation.
- That distinction is the whole reason the completeness caveat exists.
- A consumer that collapses it turns a configuration choice on a capture host into a claim about somebody's
  call.

**An unsigned container attributes nothing.** Trust it exactly as much as you
trust whoever handed it to you.

- sipnab signs an encrypted container with the key
  and certificate its operator configured.
- The signature says which operator's sipnab wrote those bytes.
- The container inside still says that sipnab observed the call and recorded nothing.

**Two containers about one call do not merge themselves.**

- sipnab writes the parties of the dialog it observed. It infers none.
- One tap on a proxied call sees two legs of one conversation, or one leg of three.
- A second tap that saw the other leg writes its own container.
- Reconciling them belongs to the consumer. The consumer is the only one holding both.

## What sipnab refuses to put in a container

Each refusal has an argument behind it in
[the design decision](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/design/vcon.md). The one-line version:

| Refused | Why |
|---|---|
| a JWS signature on an unsigned container | a signature over an observation verifies as a signature over a recording, so sipnab signs only as the inner layer of an encrypted container you configure, with your key ([Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes)) |
| consent attachments | sipnab obtained no consent, and an empty consent field reads as "none recorded" |
| lawful-basis attachments | the same, with a named regulatory reader on the other end |
| a party `name` **that sipnab vouches for** | `From` and `To` are the caller's claim about the caller, trivially spoofed |
| hosted artefacts by `url`, other than audio the operator serves | sipnab hosts nothing, so it cannot promise where a file lives. The one `url` it writes is a rule's `audio = "url"` recording, under the `audio_url_base` the operator's storage serves |

**sipnab EMITS a party `name` when the wire carried one.**

- This page previously said the Rust type has no `name` field. That was wrong.
- `Party::name` exists. It carries the display name from `From` or `To`.
- It sits alongside `sip_display_name`, never instead of it.
- It travels under the declared key. So a generic vCon
  reader shows a named party rather than an anonymous one.

What sipnab refuses is not the field but the *claim*.

- `validation` is unconditionally `"none"`.
- That says a header asserted this name and nobody checked it.

**Treat it as personal data.**

- A display name is the caller's own words about who they are.
- A container is a thing operators forward.
- If you are writing a redaction step, key it on `name` AND `sip_display_name`.
- An earlier version of this page would have led you to redact only the second.

### The message trace carries the headers, and strips the credentials

Each message in the `sip-message-trace` attachment carries a `headers` object.

- It holds the header name, and an array of its values.
- So a repeated `Via` or `Record-Route` keeps the path the message actually took.

Four headers never travel:

- `Authorization`,
- `Proxy-Authorization`,
- `WWW-Authenticate`,
- `Proxy-Authenticate`.

A digest challenge and its response are credential material. A container is a publication surface.

That filter is worth one honest sentence:

- Until 0.5.125, it did nothing. The trace carried no raw headers for it to find.
- The test guarding it passed for that reason, not because the filter worked.
- Headers, and the filter that makes them safe to publish, landed together, deliberately.
- The same test now fails if anyone drops either half.

Everything else on the wire is in the container.

- Decide whether that is acceptable for your traffic before you hand one to anybody.
- `P-Asserted-Identity`, `Diversion`, `Remote-Party-ID` and any custom header your platform sets all
  travel, exactly as the endpoint wrote them.

### One thing sipnab does supply, narrowly: `tel`

A conserver indexes parties by `tel`, `mailto` and `name`, and by nothing else.

- So a consumer can retrieve a container carrying none of the three by its UUID
  and by nothing else.
- A party search never surfaces it.
- An operator who knows only the phone number cannot find the capture.

`tel` is the only one of the three sipnab can supply from evidence.

- It supplies it only when the SIP user part is unambiguously a telephone number.
  That means `+` followed by digits, an [RFC 3966](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3966.html) global number.
- Everything else gets nothing, including bare digit runs.
  - `1001` is an extension.
  - Indexing it as a telephone number would put a wrong answer in a search index rather than no
    answer.
- The observer party never carries one at all.

### The tags that tell forked legs apart

The dialog object carries `sip_from_tag` and `sip_to_tag` when the capture
observed them.

- A Call-ID alone cannot distinguish one leg of a forked INVITE
  from another. Every fork shares it.
- So a consumer correlating legs across nodes needs the tags.

`sip_to_tag` is the `To` tag of the response that established the dialog. That is:

- a 2xx answer to the opening request,
- or, when the capture holds none, a 101-199 response to it.

sipnab falls back to a tag from a response that establishes no dialog, such as a `401` or `407` challenge.

- It does this only when the capture holds neither.
- An answer under another tag replaces it.
- [RFC 3261 section 12.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3261#section-12.1)
  is the rule.

`sip_to_tag` is absent when no message carried a `To` tag. That
is itself a signal: nothing established a dialog.

## Analyze a stored vCon

`-I` reads a vCon container the way it reads a capture.

- It reads a file, a directory of them, or a glob.
- It reads them alone or beside pcap files.
- Each SIP message the container stores is rebuilt and analyzed by the same code that analyzes
  packets.
- So all of these work on it:
  - the dialog list,
  - the ladder,
  - `--report`, `--analyze`, `--json`, `--json-dialogs`,
  - the TUI.
- The MCP tool [`analyze_vcon`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md#analyze-vcon) and
  [`POST /v1/vcon/analyze`](@/docs/api.md#post-v1-vcon-analyze) do the same for a
  container handed over inline.

### Have a container

Any container with SIP in it works. This writes one from the committed sample
capture:

```sh
sipnab -N -I sip-rtp-g711.pcap --export-vcon 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --vcon-out call.vcon.json --node-name tap-a --no-cli-print --quiet
```

It prints nothing and exits 0. It leaves `call.vcon.json` beside the capture.

### Analyze it

```sh
sipnab -N -I call.vcon.json --analyze --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Capture analysis: 1 finding(s) across 1 dialog(s), 0 stream(s), 6 frame(s) read.

THIS ANALYSIS IS INCOMPLETE — sipnab did not read all of this capture. The findings below describe what it UNDERSTOOD, so their counts are floors and the ABSENCE of a finding is not evidence that the problem is absent. The blind finding(s) are listed first.

1. [BLIND] Rebuilt from a stored vCon — 1 container(s)
   These dialogs were rebuilt from stored vCon containers, not read from packets. A vCon holds no RTP, so no media statistic here was computed, and whatever its producer did not store is absent. The evidence names each container, what it lacks, and the producer's own caveat.
   Evidence:
     - call.vcon.json, vcon 0158a120-0392-857f-8193-d90b5d03d6c4 | messages=6 | 6 SIP message(s) rebuilt from this container. Not recomputed or not stored: media: a vCon carries no RTP, so no stream, MOS, jitter or loss was computed from it; the producer's analysis holds 1 media_quality row(s), its own numbers, not recomputed; request-URI: not stored for 3 request(s), which carry sip:request-uri-not-stored.invalid; header order: the trace keys headers by name, so their order across names is the container's, not the wire's, and headers the producer did not store (credential headers, when sipnab produced it) are absent. The producer's caveat: Produced by sipnab 0.5.208 on node tap-a. sipnab OBSERVED this dialog and took no part in it: the parties below are what the From and To headers said, not identities anyone established, and nothing here is signed. No media is in this container because this run decoded none for the dialog; the capture_completeness media_note says what was measured. That is a statement about what this run kept, not a finding that the call was silent. sipnab read 852 frame(s) for this capture. No omissions recorded: every message sipnab held for this dialog is in this container. A capture-level analysis ran and ranked no blind spots.
```

The first finding is `rebuilt_from_vcon`. It is a `blind` finding.

- The analysis is of what the container stored.
- The finding names what that leaves out.
- Then it quotes the producer's own caveat.

Every message says where it came from:

```sh
sipnab -N -I call.vcon.json --json --quiet | head -1 | jq '{timestamp, src, dst, transport, method, input_origin}'
```

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2016-11-26T14:52:59.666393+00:00",
  "src": "10.0.2.20",
  "dst": "10.0.2.15",
  "transport": "UDP",
  "method": "INVITE",
  "input_origin": "vcon"
}
```

The `-N` summary line and the TUI's raw message view mark the same messages
`origin=vcon`.

### A directory of them

Write one container per INVITE dialog into `stored`. It prints
`Wrote 2 vCon container(s) to 'stored'.`

```sh
sipnab -N -I sip-rtp-g711.pcap --export-vcon-when 'method == "INVITE"' --export-vcon-dir stored --node-name tap-a --no-cli-print --quiet
```

Add a container that stores no SIP at all:

```sh
printf '{"vcon": "0.4.0", "parties": []}\n' > stored/broken.vcon.json
```

Read the directory. sipnab names the container it cannot read, with the reason.
It reads the rest:

```sh
sipnab -N -I stored --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{call_id, msg_count, final_status_code, input_origin}'
```

```text
2026-10-09T15:22:57.015657Z  WARN sipnab::capture::input_set: Skipping 'stored/broken.vcon.json': not a readable capture (a vCon container with no SIP signaling sipnab can read: it has no sip-message-trace or message/sip attachment)
2026-10-09T15:22:57.017252Z  WARN sipnab::capture::input_set: -I resolved to 2 capture file(s), 1 file(s) that are not readable captures
{"call_id":"1-1966@10.0.2.20","msg_count":6,"final_status_code":200,"input_origin":"vcon"}
{"call_id":"1-1968@10.0.2.20","msg_count":4,"final_status_code":200,"input_origin":"vcon"}
```

A container named directly with `-I` that sipnab cannot read stops the run
instead, with the same reason. A file you named is one you expected
sipnab to read.

### A container listing an extension sipnab does not support is not read

A container's `critical` parameter lists the extensions a reader must support
to interpret it.

- [Section 4.1.4 of draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.1.4)
  says a reader that does not support one "MUST NOT attempt to process or
  operate on the vCon, except to reject it or report unsupported content".
- sipnab supports the two extensions its own containers declare, `sip-signaling` and `CC`.
- sipnab skips a container whose `critical` lists anything else, as it skips a
  container without readable SIP. The reason names each unsupported extension.
- `analyze_vcon` and `POST /v1/vcon/analyze` answer `verdict: unreadable` with
  that reason. They run no schema check.
- `validate_vcon` and `POST /v1/vcon/validate` refuse the container.

### A container the schema refuses is still read

What sipnab skips is a container whose SIP it cannot read.

- Some containers disagree with the vendored draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema but store
  readable SIP. Such a container still reads.
- sipnab reports the finding with it.
- The common case is a container that went through vcon.store. vcon.store hands `extensions` back as an
  object rather than the array the schema requires:

```sh
jq '.extensions = {"sip-signaling": true, "CC": true}' call.vcon.json > store-shape.vcon.json
```

```sh
sipnab -N -I store-shape.vcon.json --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{call_id, msg_count, input_origin}'
```

```text
2026-10-09T15:22:57.067344Z  WARN sipnab::capture::file: 'store-shape.vcon.json' fails the draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema (/extensions (type): expected type "array", found object); its SIP is read regardless, and the analysis carries the finding(s)
{"call_id":"1-1966@10.0.2.20","msg_count":6,"input_origin":"vcon"}
```

The `rebuilt_from_vcon` finding in `--analyze` carries the same schema finding
for that container. The MCP tool and the REST route list it in
`schema_findings`.

### What sipnab reads, and what cannot come back

- **Two stored forms.**
  - The first is the `sip-message-trace` attachment sipnab writes, and
    the trace form of draft-howe-vcon-sip-signaling-00 it extends.
    These give each message its time, addresses, ports and transport.
  - The second is `message/sip` attachments, the draft's other form.
    - They carry each message whole, timed by the attachment's `start`.
    - That form stores no addressing. So those messages carry
      `0.0.0.0:0`, and the finding says so.
  - A container with neither form holds nothing to analyze.
    An example is the recording-only example in core-04 Appendix A.
    sipnab skips it with that reason.
- **Detection is by content.**
  - sipnab reads a file whose first character other
    than whitespace is `{` as a container, whatever its name.
  - Some JSON objects have none of the members a vCon has (`vcon`, `uuid`, `created_at`, `parties`,
    `dialog`, `analysis`, `attachments`). Such an object is not one. sipnab skips it with
    that reason.
  - `extensions` counts in either form, the core-04 array or the
    vcon.store object.
- **sipnab skips unreadable SIP, not a schema finding.**
  - It skips a container with no `sip-message-trace` or `message/sip` attachment, naming the reason.
  - It also skips a container whose attachments
    hold no message it can rebuild, naming the reason.
  - It reads a container that fails the schema and stores readable SIP. It reports the finding.
- **One container is at most 64 MiB.**
  - sipnab reads a container whole to validate it.
  - So it refuses a file larger than `MAX_CONTAINER_BYTES`
    (67,108,864 bytes) without reading it. It names the size and the limit.
  - As with any container it cannot read, sipnab skips it in a directory or a glob.
    It stops the run when you name it directly.
  - A container carrying inline audio within
    the 5 MiB default budget is far below the limit.
- **No media.**
  - A vCon stores no RTP. So sipnab computes no stream, MOS,
    jitter or loss from it.
  - It reports no media fault for a call that had none
    to measure.
  - `analyze_vcon` and `POST /v1/vcon/analyze` return the producer's
    own `media_quality` numbers verbatim, as its numbers.
- **No request-URI.** The trace stores the method, not the request line.
  - So a rebuilt request carries `sip:request-uri-not-stored.invalid`.
  - That is a name in the reserved `.invalid` domain.
- **Some things do not come back:**
  - header order across names,
  - bodies other than SDP,
  - headers the producer did not store (sipnab removes credential headers).
  - `Content-Length` states the body the container holds.
- **No frame pointers.** A rebuilt message was never a frame anyone can read
  again. So it carries none.
- **`--redact`ed containers** read back with their pseudonyms. Nothing can
  recover the originals from them.
- **Not with `--cores` or a BPF filter.**
  - `--cores` shards captured frames. A BPF filter selects them.
  - A container holds neither. So sipnab refuses both, with the reason.
  - Select dialogs with `--filter` instead.
- **sipnab sends nothing anywhere.** The addresses in a container are a record
  of a finished call. So sipnab never transmits a response to them.

## What this does not do

Stated here rather than discovered later.

- **It does not host audio.**
  - When the run retained the RTP payload, the container carries the audio INLINE.
    It is a `recording` Dialog Object with a `sha512-` content hash.
  - A rule with `audio = "url"` instead writes the WAV file beside the container.
    It names the file by a `url` under the rule's `audio_url_base`, with the
    `content_hash` of the WAV file and no body.
  - The operator's storage serves that URL. sipnab does not check that it does.
  - A `--redact` export never names a `url`.
  - When the run retained no audio, the container says so in words and carries none.

  Audio over the inline budget draws an out-loud refusal rather than a silent truncation.

  - `--vcon-max-inline-media` sets that budget in MiB. It defaults to 5.
  - That figure comes from a measurement against a real vCon store. The store:
    - answered `204` for a container of roughly 12 MB,
    - wrote it to its database,
    - had its own file spool refuse the payload,
    - and neither side reported the partial write.
  - `0` refuses every inline body without turning the exporter off.

  sipnab retains whole calls. So a call's audio grows with its length.

  - A two-way 20 ms G.711 call exports as 8 kHz stereo. That is 32,000 bytes of WAV a
    second.
  - It fits the 5 MiB default for up to 122 seconds.
  - At 123 seconds, the container carries the refusal instead.
  - Raise `--vcon-max-inline-media` to what the store you send to accepts.
    Or write the WAV beside the container with the `export_audio` MCP tool.

  A `--redact` export carries no audio at all.

  - Redaction deletes audio rather than replacing it with a token.
  - Its Dialog Object is the signaling one, typed by the rule above.
  - `capture_completeness.media` says `withheld-by-redaction`.

  Every door (batch export, REST and MCP) reads the one value.
  So the same call cannot come back carrying
  audio through one and a refusal through another.
- **It ties the legs of a B2BUA call together only by its correlation.**
  - With `grouping = "leg"`, the default, two Call-IDs produce two containers.
    Each names the other in its `sipnab-related-legs` attachment, with the
    strategy that tied them.
  - With `grouping = "call"` one container holds every leg the rule selects.
  - A tie that is a timing guess carries `identifier_match: false`. A busy
    server can get it wrong.
  - See [Calls through a PBX or a B2BUA](#calls-through-a-pbx-or-a-b2bua).
- **It does not assemble a call across hops.** One container describes one
  observed dialog from one capture.
- **It does not deduplicate across taps.**
  - Two sipnab boxes that saw the same dialog mint different uuids.
  - The uuid mixes in the node and the capture identity along with the Call-ID.
- **Its uuid is a function of the dialog, the node and the capture, not a
  random value.**
  - The 48-bit timestamp is the dialog's first observed message.
  - The other 74 bits are digests. `rand_a` (12 bits) digests the Call-ID and
    the capture identity. `rand_b` (62 bits) digests the node name, the Call-ID
    and the capture identity.
  - Two dialogs that opened in the same millisecond on one node differ in those 74 bits.
  - Re-exporting one dialog from one capture yields the same uuid. So
    deduplication on `uuid` is safe for re-exports. That is what it exists for.
  - Until 0.5.125 `rand_b` digested the node alone. That left 12 bits to
    separate such dialogs.
- **It does not store anything.** sipnab writes a container and forgets it.
  There is no vCon store, no index, no retention.
